nodes.label: 2-D Prefix Sums (Inclusion-Exclusion)
nodes.rationale: The -p[i-1][j-1] in the build and the +p[r1][c1] in the query are the same inclusion-exclusion correction for the doubly-counted corner. Foundation of integral images and Viola-Jones face detection.

nodes.label: Prefix Sums + HashMap (Subarray Sum with Negatives)
nodes.rationale: sum(l..r)==k iff prefix[l]==prefix[r]-k, so counting subarrays becomes counting earlier prefix values in Theta(1). Theta(n) and sign-agnostic — the fix for the sliding-window limitation — and generalizes to divisibility (key on running % k) and balance problems.
nodes.norm_label: prefix sums + hashmap (subarray sum with negatives)

nodes.label: Fenwick over a Difference Array
nodes.rationale: Range update with point query in two calls — add(l,+v), add(r+1,-v), and a point query becomes a prefix sum. The cheapest trick in the topic; no lazy propagation needed.

nodes.label: Fenwick Tree (Binary Indexed Tree)
nodes.rationale: tree[i] holds the aggregate of the i & (-i) elements ending at i — each index owns a range the length of its lowest set bit. One array of size n, no pointers, no recursion. Measured 3.9 ms vs ~5,623 ms naive rescan (~1,400x) for 100k interleaved updates and queries over n=10^6, and the ratio grows linearly with n.

nodes.label: Segment Tree
nodes.rationale: Stores a genuine aggregate per range node and answers by COMBINING Theta(log n) disjoint nodes rather than subtracting two prefixes — so no inverse is required and any associative operation works. Costs 2n memory and a larger constant; earns it only for non-invertible ops or lazy range updates.

nodes.label: Slices & Split Borrows
nodes.rationale: Many structures need no nodes at all — heaps, union-find, Fenwick trees, hash tables are arrays with arithmetic. split_at_mut, chunks_mut, and get_disjoint_mut (stable 1.86) prove disjointness statically.

nodes.label: Largest Rectangle in a Histogram
nodes.rationale: Canonical Theta(n) application: a bar's rectangle extends to previous-smaller and next-smaller, both computed in one monotonic-stack pass; the pop is where the area is computed.

nodes.label: Sparse Table
nodes.rationale: st[k][i] covers 2^k elements from i; a query uses two OVERLAPPING blocks, which is safe only because the operation is idempotent (min, max, gcd). Theta(1) queries at Theta(n log n) space and no updates at all.

nodes.label: Deque Operation Ordering (maintain back, evict front, read front)
nodes.rationale: Only one ordering of the three per-iteration operations is correct; reading the front before evicting reports a maximum outside the window, and the bug is rare in random data because it needs the max exactly at the expiring position. Keep the naive Theta(n*k) version as a permanent test oracle.
nodes.norm_label: deque operation ordering (maintain back, evict front, read front)

nodes.label: Monotonic Deque (Sliding Window Max)
nodes.rationale: Indices increasing, values decreasing so the front is the window max. Measured k-independent (11.35 ms at k=100 vs 11.20 ms at k=10,000) on n=1,000,000 — the signature of the technique. The heap was within 10% at large k, so the honest wins are k-independence and Theta(k) memory, not a large constant factor.

nodes.label: Monotonic Stack
nodes.rationale: Discards elements that can never be the answer again: if v[j] > v[i] and j > i, v[i] is dominated. Converts Theta(n^2) into Theta(n) because each element is pushed once and popped at most once. The pop IS where the answer is recorded.

nodes.label: Store Indices, Not Values
nodes.rationale: Every maintenance rule is positional — window expiry, left boundary — and positions are only recoverable from indices. Also the only formulation that handles duplicate values correctly.

nodes.label: Difference Array
nodes.rationale: The exact dual of prefix sums — prefix-sum and difference are discrete integration and differentiation. Range updates become two point updates: Theta(n+u) where naive is Theta(n*u). The 'invert it' lens.

nodes.label: Invertibility Requirement
nodes.rationale: prefix[r]-prefix[l] works because addition has an inverse. Min and max do not: from min(0..r)=3 and min(0..l)=3 you cannot determine min(l..r). Sums, XOR (self-inverse), counts, and non-zero products work; min/max/gcd need a sparse table or segment tree.

nodes.label: Prefix Sum Array
nodes.rationale: Precompute once, query Theta(1). n+1 entries with prefix[0]=0 and half-open ranges is not a convention but what makes prefix[r]-prefix[l] work for every l<=r without a special case — and it matches Rust's &a[l..r] slice convention as a continual consistency check.

nodes.label: Decision Rule: Does the Data Change?
nodes.rationale: The entire hierarchy exists to make UPDATES cheap; with no updates you pay for a capability you don't use, and pay in the query path. Static data: prefix sums are three lines, Theta(1), and FASTER than a tree (2 reads vs ~20 scattered). Ask this first, not last.
nodes.norm_label: decision rule: does the data change?

nodes.label: Fenwick 1-Indexing Encapsulation
nodes.rationale: The structure depends on the lowest set bit and 0 has none, so i -= i & (-i) at i=0 is an infinite loop. Keep the 1-indexing strictly inside the type and expose a 0-indexed half-open API so the conversion happens in exactly one place.

nodes.label: Hierarchy of Overlapping Blocks
nodes.rationale: Precompute aggregates over a hierarchy of blocks instead of over every prefix: a range decomposes into Theta(log n) precomputed pieces and a point update touches only the Theta(log n) blocks containing it. That single idea produces Fenwick, segment tree, and sqrt decomposition — they differ only in which hierarchy they use.

nodes.label: Separate Left/Right Accumulators for Non-Commutative Ops
nodes.rationale: The iterative bottom-up query walks in from both ends; one accumulator combines pieces out of order. Harmless for + and min, silently wrong for matrix products or string concatenation — so the bug appears only when the structure is reused, long after it was trusted.

nodes.label: Persistence Levels (Partial / Full / Confluent)
nodes.rationale: Confluent persistence is harder than full because merging can create sharing patterns that break the Theta(log n) bound. Git with merges is confluently persistent.

nodes.label: RRB-Tree (Persistent Vector)
nodes.rationale: 32-way branching trie indexed by position: Theta(log32 n) index/update/push/pop plus Theta(log n) concatenation and slicing, which a flat Vec cannot do at all. The 'relaxed' part (partially full nodes) is what makes concatenation efficient.

nodes.label: Arc::make_mut Copy-on-Write

nodes.label: CAS on the Root When Publishing a Version
nodes.rationale: Immutability makes reading lock-free but 'derive a new version and store it' is a read-modify-write on the shared root pointer, which is not atomic just because the data is immutable. Two threads deriving from one root silently lose an update. Fix: compare-and-swap on the root, retrying if the base changed — the same optimistic-concurrency pattern as expected_version in event sourcing.

nodes.label: Immutable Structures Are Sync For Free
nodes.rationale: Arc<Node> with no interior mutability is Send + Sync, so a persistent structure is concurrently readable with zero synchronization. That property, not the versioning, is what makes it worth its 2-10x read constant factor in Rust.
nodes.norm_label: immutable structures are sync for free

nodes.label: Accidentally Retained Versions
nodes.rationale: Because every version shares structure, a single retained old root pins all structure reachable from it. Memory grows without bound and profiling shows no leak because every allocation is genuinely reachable. Bound the version history explicitly.

nodes.label: Structural Sharing
nodes.rationale: An update copies only the root-to-change path and shares every untouched subtree by reference, so versioning costs proportional to the change (Theta(log n)) rather than to the data (Theta(n)).

nodes.label: Randomness Replaces Balance Logic
nodes.rationale: A treap maintains balance with a random priority per node instead of rotation-counting case analysis (~20 lines vs red-black's); a skip list replaces rebalancing with coin flips and is far easier to make lock-free. You trade a worst-case guarantee for expected behaviour and get a large reduction in code complexity.

nodes.label: Aliasing XOR Mutability
nodes.rationale: Every textbook data structure assumes many mutable pointers into one node graph — precisely what the borrow checker forbids. The five representation strategies are five different answers to how you build a linked structure under this one rule.

nodes.label: Arena + Index Handles
nodes.rationale: An index is not a borrow — that is the whole trick. Arbitrary topology (cycles, back-pointers, cross-links) becomes trivially expressible, plus half the memory (u32 vs 8-byte pointers), contiguity for the prefetcher, Copy handles, and free serialization. The default for this category.

nodes.label: Rc<RefCell<T>> Shared Mutable Nodes
nodes.rationale: The closest syntactic analogue to a C pointer, so it is what a C/Java/Python instinct reaches for — and it compiles immediately, which feels like validation. But it converts compile-time errors into runtime BorrowMutError panics, adds refcount traffic, and leaks on cycles without Weak. The borrow checker didn't approve the design; it was turned off.

nodes.label: Recursive Drop Stack Overflow
nodes.rationale: The derived Drop for Box<Node> recurses one frame per link. Measured release, 8 MB main stack: fine at 250,000 nodes, aborts at 300,000 (~30 bytes/frame); a 2 MB spawned thread fails ~4x sooner, so code that survives on main dies in a worker. Fix with an iterative Drop using Option::take(), or an arena where no recursion exists.

nodes.label: Maintain a Structure, Don't Recompute a Statistic
nodes.rationale: Selection is one-shot over a static array and has no incremental form, because its whole speed comes from destructively partitioning the data it was given. Over m updates, re-selecting is Theta(n*m). Two heaps give a running median in Theta(log n); a Fenwick or order-statistic tree gives rank queries over a changing set.
nodes.norm_label: maintain a structure, don't recompute a statistic

nodes.label: Bitmask Search State
nodes.rationale: N-queens tracks columns and both diagonals as u32 masks; diagonals shift by one per row so d1<<1 and d2>>1 propagate attacks automatically. Feasibility for a whole row is one AND, and candidates are iterated with the x & -x lowest-set-bit trick — why 9-queens ran in 50 us.

nodes.label: A* Search
nodes.rationale: Dijkstra with priority dist[v] + h(v). Admissible h (never overestimates) gives optimality; additionally consistent h finalizes each vertex once, exactly as in Dijkstra. With h == 0 it IS Dijkstra.

nodes.label: DAG Relaxation
nodes.rationale: Topological order already guarantees every predecessor is finalized before a vertex is reached — the exact guarantee Dijkstra's heap works to establish. Theta(V+E), allows negative weights, and is the only way to get LONGEST path (by negating). Silently wrong on a cyclic graph, so use Kahn's algorithm which detects the cycle as a by-product.

nodes.label: Dijkstra's Algorithm
nodes.rationale: Always finalize the closest unfinished vertex; its distance can never improve because reaching it via any other vertex means going further first. The proof step that fails with a negative edge is '<= the whole path's length' — a longer prefix can yield a shorter total, and Dijkstra returns wrong answers with no error. Measured 56.34 ms with a binary heap vs 78.92 s with an O(V^2) scan at V=200k, E=1M (1,401x).

nodes.label: Average-Case vs Expected-Case
nodes.rationale: Randomness converts a promise about your input into a promise about your coin flips — and you control the coins. Average-case quantifies over an assumed input distribution the adversary is not drawing from; expected-case quantifies over the algorithm's own randomness and holds on EVERY input.

nodes.label: CSPRNG vs Fast PRNG
nodes.rationale: Non-cryptographic PRNGs are designed for statistical quality, not unpredictability — xorshift's full state is recoverable from a handful of outputs and a timestamp seed has ~2^30 realistic values. Nothing in the type system marks this, so the rule is per-use-site: OsRng/getrandom for tokens, nonces, keys, salts.

nodes.label: Seed Reproducibility in Tests and Benchmarks
nodes.rationale: Randomness is a hidden input: a test's outcome depends on it as much as on the code, so an unrecorded failing run is unreconstructible. Seed with StdRng::seed_from_u64 and print the seed on failure; proptest persists failing seeds automatically, giving exploration and reproducibility together.
nodes.norm_label: seed reproducibility in tests and benchmarks

nodes.label: Lazy Propagation
nodes.rationale: Maintains a second invariant — a node's aggregate is correct assuming all pending ancestor updates have been applied — so every access path must push down first and pull up after. Funnel all node access through push_down/pull_up helpers so skipping is structurally impossible, then property-test with a brute-force checker.

nodes.label: Pruning Is the Entire Algorithm
nodes.rationale: A rejection at depth d removes n^(n-d) leaves at once, so pruning changes the BASE of the exponent rather than shaving a constant. Measured N-queens: 50.38 us vs 2.20 s at n=9 (43,580x), growing from 305x at n=6 — so for backtracking, measure; don't estimate from the bound.

nodes.label: Make/Unmake State Restoration
nodes.rationale: At every search node the partial assignment is consistent and mutable state is exactly restored on the way back up. The make/unmake pair is separated by the recursive call, so any continue, early return, or ? skips the undo — the same shape as a missing free, and the compiler cannot help. Make it structurally unskippable with adjacency or a Drop guard.

nodes.label: Memoization Converts Backtracking into DP
nodes.rationale: The recursion tree has Theta(2^n) nodes but only Theta(n) distinct states; a two-line memo converts exponential to polynomial. Measured naive Fibonacci at n=40: 312.84 ms vs 333 ns with an array memo (~939,000x), and an array memo beat a HashMap memo by 13.4x because integer-indexed states need no hashing.

nodes.label: Rust Does Not Guarantee Tail-Call Optimization
nodes.rationale: LLVM often does it in release when no destructors must run at the call site, but Drop semantics frequently prevent exactly that — and it is absent in debug builds where you would first hit the overflow. Write the loop.
nodes.norm_label: rust does not guarantee tail-call optimization

nodes.label: Recursion as an Inductive Proof
nodes.rationale: Two obligations and nothing else: base case correct, and inductive step correct ASSUMING smaller inputs work — plus progress under a well-founded measure. The practical skill is to stop tracing the call stack and check the obligations.

nodes.label: Recursion Depth Guard / Explicit Stack
nodes.rationale: The call stack is a fixed-size resource guarded by an unmapped page; overflow ABORTS and cannot be caught. Measured ~100k frames survive and 200k aborts on the 8 MB main thread, ~4x sooner on a 2 MB spawned thread, while an explicit stack handled 5,000,000. The trigger is input-controlled depth, not recursion itself.

nodes.label: Choose the Hasher by Key Provenance
nodes.rationale: The hasher feels like a global default but is a per-map security/performance trade. Self-generated keys (indices, interned symbols) -> FxHashMap/aHash, measured 4.6-6.0x faster for u32 keys but only 1.2-1.3x for 16-char Strings. Anything attacker-reachable keeps std's RandomState, whose random per-process seed makes precomputed collision attacks impossible.
nodes.norm_label: choose the hasher by key provenance

nodes.label: Extended Euclidean Algorithm
nodes.source_location: The six routines worth writing once
nodes.rationale: Computes an inverse for any b coprime to m and reports failure when gcd(b,m) != 1, rather than returning garbage the way a Fermat modpow would with a composite modulus.

nodes.label: Modular Inverse via Fermat's Little Theorem
nodes.source_location: The six routines worth writing once
nodes.rationale: inv(a) = a^(m-2) mod m requires m PRIME. With a composite modulus it is silently wrong for any b not coprime to m — and right for coprime b, so tests often pass. Measured: 100,000 inverses took 23.1 ms.
nodes.norm_label: modular inverse via fermat's little theorem

nodes.label: Modular Exponentiation (modpow / exponentiation by squaring)
nodes.source_location: The six routines worth writing once
nodes.rationale: Theta(log e) and works for any associative operation — integers, matrices, function composition. Must compute in u128 because two values below 10^9+7 multiply to nearly 10^18.

nodes.label: nCr with Precomputed Factorials
nodes.source_location: The six routines worth writing once
nodes.rationale: The inverse-factorial trick: compute inv_fact[n] with ONE modpow, then walk backwards with inv_fact[i-1] = inv_fact[i] * i. Theta(n + log m) instead of Theta(n log m).

nodes.label: Matrix Exponentiation for Linear Recurrences
nodes.rationale: A k-term linear recurrence becomes a k x k matrix power, giving Theta(k^3 log n) — n = 10^18 is ~60 matrix multiplications. The dynamic-programming 'amortize it' lens taken to its conclusion.

nodes.label: Bellman-Ford
nodes.rationale: After k rounds dist[v] is correct for every vertex whose shortest path uses at most k edges; a simple path has at most V-1 edges, so V-1 rounds suffice — and a V-th improving round means a reachable negative cycle. That detection is not a bolt-on; it falls out of the invariant.

nodes.label: Currency Arbitrage as a Negative Cycle
nodes.rationale: Taking -log(rate) as the weight turns a product condition into a sum condition, so an arbitrage opportunity is exactly a negative cycle — the canonical reason to care about negative-cycle detection.
nodes.norm_label: currency arbitrage as a negative cycle

nodes.label: Floyd-Warshall
nodes.rationale: The k loop must be outermost — it is the DP over 'paths using only intermediates from {0..k}'. Simple, cache-friendly, and genuinely right for V <= ~500; for sparse graphs Dijkstra-from-every-vertex wins, and Johnson's handles negatives by reweighting with Bellman-Ford first.

nodes.label: Modular Arithmetic
nodes.rationale: Turns unbounded numbers into fixed-size ones while preserving ring structure. Division is not well-defined — it needs an inverse, which exists iff gcd(b,m)=1, which is why prime moduli like 10^9+7 and 998244353 are ubiquitous.

nodes.label: Overflow Before the Modulus (u128 reduction)
nodes.rationale: The modulus is applied after the multiplication, so the intermediate must fit. u64 holds one product of two sub-10^9 values but not three. Fix: compute in u128, or wrap the modulus in a newtype so every operation reduces by construction. Montgomery/Barrett reduction is the after-measurement optimization.

nodes.label: Rust % is a Remainder, Not a Modulus
nodes.rationale: % takes the sign of the dividend, so (a - b) % m is negative when a < b — a negative index panic or wrong branch. Always (a + m - b) % m, or rem_euclid.
nodes.norm_label: rust % is a remainder, not a modulus

nodes.label: Widen the Prefix Array Type
nodes.rationale: The prefix array's magnitude grows with n, not with the element range — it is a fundamentally larger quantity built from the same values. Always i64/u64 prefix over i32 data.

nodes.label: Infinity Sentinel Overflow
nodes.rationale: u64::MAX is the natural spelling of infinity and also the value that overflows on any addition, so unreached vertices appear at distance ~0 in release. Only fires on disconnected graphs, which random connected test graphs never exercise. Guard the relaxation, use MAX/2, or Option<u64>.

nodes.label: Relaxation
nodes.rationale: Every shortest-path algorithm is the same operation applied in a different order — nothing else happens. dist[v] is always the length of SOME path (an upper bound) and relaxation only decreases it; the algorithm terminates when no edge can be relaxed. The choice of which edge to relax next determines both cost and what the algorithm can handle.

nodes.label: Sieve of Eratosthenes
nodes.source_location: The six routines worth writing once
nodes.rationale: Batch algorithm: Theta(n log log n) for all primes <= n. Two details halve the work — start marking at i^2, stop the outer loop at sqrt(n). Measured 20.49 ms for primes below 10^7 (664,579 primes), ~172x faster than trial division.

nodes.label: slice::select_nth_unstable
nodes.rationale: Introselect: starts with a fast pivot strategy and falls back to a guaranteed-Theta(n) method on poor splits, so the worst case is bounded regardless of input. Measured 1.21 ms vs 13.01 ms for a full sort on top-10 of 1M u64 (10.7x). It reorders the whole slice, so preserving the input costs a clone.

nodes.label: Miller-Rabin Primality Test
nodes.rationale: Single-number test at Theta(k log^3 n) with error 4^-k; size-bound rather than range-bound, which is the opposite of a sieve. Choosing wrongly is 100x in one direction and impossible in the other.

nodes.label: Las Vegas vs Monte Carlo
nodes.rationale: Las Vegas: always correct, random runtime — the guarantee is on expected time. Monte Carlo: always fast, may be wrong with bounded probability — the guarantee is on the error rate, and errors are independent per run so k rounds give eps^k.

nodes.label: Median-of-Medians (BFPRT)
nodes.rationale: Groups of 5 guarantee a pivot between the 30th and 70th percentile, bounding the recursion — the proof that Theta(n) worst-case selection is possible. Its ~10-20x constant means nobody runs it directly; it is the fallback that makes introselect's guarantee real, the same relationship heapsort has with introsort.

nodes.label: Quickselect
nodes.rationale: Partitioning tells you which side the answer is on, so you recurse into ONE side: n + n/2 + n/4 + ... = 2n instead of n log n. The recursive call is in tail position, so write it as a loop and the space is Theta(1).

nodes.label: Error Amplification by Repetition
nodes.rationale: Repeating a Monte Carlo algorithm with FRESH randomness drives error down exponentially: Miller-Rabin's 1/4 per round becomes 4^-k, and 40 rounds is ~10^-24 — below the probability of a cosmic-ray bit flip.

nodes.label: Ord / Hash / Eq Trait Contracts
nodes.source_location: Trait contracts you must not break
nodes.rationale: These are contracts, not just signatures — the compiler checks shape, never semantics. A non-total Ord makes BTreeMap silently lose entries; disagreeing Hash/Eq makes entries unfindable. Floats are the standard trap: partial_cmp().unwrap() panics on NaN, so use f64::total_cmp or ordered-float, and property-test the laws with proptest.

nodes.label: Partition Postcondition (Neither Side Is Sorted)
nodes.rationale: 'Partial sort' is a misleading label. select_nth_unstable guarantees a PARTITION — everything before k is <= v[k], everything after is >= it — and establishing order within the prefix is precisely the work it skips, which is why it is Theta(n). Passing &v[..k] to a binary search is silently wrong.

nodes.label: Three-Way (Dutch Flag) Partition
nodes.rationale: All-equal input is the sneakiest quadratic trigger because a two-way partition puts every element on one side — so the fix is a PARTITIONING change, not a pivot change. Costs speed on data with no duplicates.

nodes.label: Integer-Scaled Edge Weights
nodes.rationale: f64 isn't Ord so it can't go in a BinaryHeap without NotNan, and float addition isn't associative — two equal-length paths can compare unequal, making results depend on traversal order. Scaling to millimetres/milliseconds/cents removes both problems.

nodes.rationale: The arena reintroduces use-after-free as a logic bug: a freed-and-reused slot makes an old Handle(7) silently name a different node. {idx, gen} with the generation bumped on reuse converts silent corruption into a visible None at the point of use. 4 extra bytes per handle and slot.

nodes.label: HAMT (Hash Array Mapped Trie)
nodes.rationale: A trie over hash bits with 32-way branching: a 32-bit bitmap plus a packed child array, indexed via popcount(bitmap & ((1<<i)-1)). ~4 levels for 1M entries, and branching on hash bits gives uniform depth regardless of key distribution.

nodes.label: Bloom Filter
nodes.source_location: Bloom filter — sizing is the whole design
nodes.rationale: One-sided error: all k bits set means maybe present, any bit clear means definitely absent — because insertion only ever sets bits, which is also why you cannot delete. Measured FP matched theory to within 0.01 percentage points; ~4.8 bits/item divides the FP rate by 10. Space is independent of item size but NOT of n, so it saturates silently on an unbounded stream.

nodes.label: Count-Min Sketch
nodes.rationale: d rows of w counters; the estimate min_i sketch[i][h_i(x)] only ever over-estimates because collisions only add. Safe for heavy hitters ('definitely at least this frequent'), unsafe for 'is this rare'.

nodes.label: Cuckoo Filter
nodes.rationale: Stores fingerprints in a cuckoo hash table: supports deletion natively and is often smaller than a Bloom below ~1% FP. The modern default when deletion is needed, at the cost of an insertion failure mode near full and a weaker merge story.

nodes.label: HyperLogLog
nodes.rationale: Each register stores a MAXIMUM number of leading zeros, so it is idempotent — which is exactly what makes it count distinct items and what makes it merge by element-wise max. Measured: 16 KB (p=14) counted 10,000,000 distinct to 0.41%, and the memory is identical for 1,000 or 10 billion.

nodes.label: Sqrt Decomposition
nodes.rationale: Theta(sqrt n) — ~1,000 ops at n=10^6 vs a segment tree's ~20 — but trivially adaptable to weird aggregates (range mode, distinct count) where no logarithmic structure is obvious. Mo's algorithm builds on it for offline query batching.

nodes.label: Sketches Store a Function of the Data, Not the Data
nodes.rationale: Give up exactness and space collapses from proportional-to-the-data to proportional-to-the-accuracy-you-asked-for. Three checks in order: which direction does the error go, is it mergeable, does the bound hold in practice.

nodes.label: Streaming Top-k via Size-k Min-Heap
nodes.rationale: When n is unknown you cannot partition at all, because partitioning requires the whole array. A min-heap of size k has its root as the k-th largest, so most elements are rejected after one comparison: Theta(n log k) time, Theta(k) space, near-Theta(n) in practice for k << n.

nodes.label: t-digest / DDSketch (Mergeable Quantiles)
nodes.rationale: Bounded relative error in Theta(1/eps) space, accurate at the tails, and mergeable — the only correct way to get a global p99 from per-host data.

nodes.label: Mergeability (Merge Sketches, Then Query)
nodes.rationale: Distinct-count and quantiles are not linear functionals, so estimates cannot be summed or averaged. Merging must happen on the sketch representation where the mathematics is defined: HLL by element-wise max (exact), Bloom by OR, Count-Min by add. Ship the sketch, not the estimate — and all hosts must agree on parameters, which becomes a versioning problem.

nodes.label: Never Average Percentiles
nodes.rationale: Percentiles are not linear so they do not average — the p99 of a union is not a function of the per-part p99s, and one skewed host can dominate the global tail while its own p99 looks unremarkable. Averaging systematically understates the true p99, so SLOs get made on a fiction. Merge sketches centrally instead.

nodes.label: The Fibonacci Heap Trap
nodes.rationale: Theta(E + V log V) is asymptotically better than a binary heap's Theta((V+E) log V) and loses in practice — pointer-chasing, allocation, and cache behaviour swamp the improvement. Use a binary heap with lazy deletion.

nodes.label: Lazy Deletion in the Priority Queue
nodes.rationale: Push a duplicate on improvement instead of decrease-key, and discard stale entries on pop with `if d > dist[u] { continue; }`. That guard is load-bearing, not an optimization: measured 49% of pops are stale. The usual 'heap grows to Theta(E)' claim is a worst case — measured pushes were 2.0xV, because a vertex is re-pushed only when its distance actually improves, so an indexed heap solves a problem that mostly isn't there.
